cards.title: The Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Sparse Halfspaces
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C≥2 and a,b>0 such that, for every n≥2 and 1≤r≤n, SQ-DIM(Hn,r, 1/[C(r log₂ n)^a])≤C n^b, where Hn,r is the class of r-sparse halfspaces on {0,1}ⁿ and SQ-DIM is the distribution-worst-case correlation parameter defined below?
cards.why: Clarifies whether a statistical-query learner can exploit sparsity while tolerating coarse, sample-efficient estimates. The problem isolates an informational obstruction from the cost of reading many irrelevant coordinates, without assuming a favorable data distribution.
cards.status_note: Source Problem 3 and its definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. No resolution of this worst-distribution, inverse-poly(r log n) parameter question was located. Results for noisy, Gaussian, smoothed or ordinary sample-access learning do not automatically settle it. No exhaustive literature or proof audit is claimed.

sentences: An r-sparse halfspace uses at most r of the n Boolean input coordinates.
Statistical-query learning accesses approximate expectations instead of individual labeled examples.
The source asks whether the worst-case number of nearly uncorrelated sparse halfspaces stays polynomial in n when correlation is inverse-polynomial in r log n.
Both the sparsity dependence and the worst-case distribution are essential to the question.
A resolution would clarify the informational limits of exploiting sparse structure through statistical queries.

cards.definitions: A member of Hn,r is a function h:{0,1}ⁿ→{−1,+1} of the form h(x)=+1 if ∑j wⱼxⱼ≥θ and h(x)=−1 otherwise, where w∈ℝⁿ has at most r nonzero coordinates and θ∈ℝ. Different weight representations of the same function define one member. For any probability distribution D on the finite cube and 0<γ<1, SQ-DIM(Hn,r,D,γ) is the largest integer d for which there are d distinct functions h₁,…,hd in Hn,r satisfying |∑x D(x)hᵢ(x)hⱼ(x)|≤γ whenever i≠j. Then SQ-DIM(Hn,r,γ) is the maximum of this integer over all D, without any uniformity, product-distribution or margin promise. These maxima exist because the Boolean function class is finite and each feasible correlation condition is a closed constraint on the finite probability simplex. The constants C,a,b must work simultaneously for all n,r and all distributions. This is exactly the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial parameter question in source Problem 3, with its O(1) exponents made explicit. It asks for an upper bound on this dimension, not polynomial time to enumerate the functions or evaluate real weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound for some fixed C,a,b, or prove its negation: for every choice of such constants there are n,r and a distribution supporting a family larger than Cn^b with pairwise absolute correlations at most 1/[C(r log₂ n)^a]. The target is this source-defined parameter statement, not a guarantee restricted to one distribution or to halfspaces with large margin.

context_blocks.title: Learning with many irrelevant coordinates
context_blocks.text: A sparse halfspace uses at most r of n coordinates, even though the learner does not know which ones matter. For example, a rule depending only on x₇ is one-sparse regardless of how many other features are supplied. Attribute efficiency asks whether learning can benefit from this sparsity without requiring labeled information proportional to every coordinate.

context_blocks.title: What a statistical query reveals
context_blocks.text: An SQ learner asks for an approximate expectation of a bounded function φ(x,h(x))∈[−1,1]. A tolerance τ allows any answer within τ of the true expectation. Smaller tolerance requires more precise information. The source relates inverse-polynomial tolerance in r log n to attribute-efficient use of labeled examples.

context_blocks.title: Why nearly uncorrelated functions appear
context_blocks.text: Under the uniform distribution, the one-sparse rules 2x₁−1 and 2x₂−1 have correlation zero: they agree as often as they disagree. SQ-DIM asks how many candidate halfspaces can be almost uncorrelated at once under the same distribution. It then takes the worst distribution, which need not be uniform.

context_blocks.title: The two polynomial requirements differ
context_blocks.text: The allowed correlation scale is inverse-polynomial in r log n, while the required bound on the number of nearly uncorrelated functions is polynomial in n. Replacing the latter with a polynomial in r log n would ask for a stronger statement. Allowing inverse-polynomial tolerance in n instead would change the intended attribute-efficiency regime.

context_blocks.title: What the source result establishes
context_blocks.text: The source gives bounds connecting this correlation parameter to weak SQ learning. Its discussion of converting weak learning to high accuracy additionally allows unlabeled samples. The exact Problem 3 dimension question keeps those access models distinct.

cards.title: Can Local Regularization Learn All Multiclass Problems?
cards.formal: Does every realizably PAC-learnable multiclass hypothesis class H admit a fixed local regularizer ψ:H×X→ℝ≥0 such that every learner induced by ψ, under the pointwise minimum-score rule below, PAC learns H? This is the existence part of the source question; optimal sample complexity is a separate refinement.
cards.why: Tests whether a fixed preference over hypotheses at each prediction point is a general principle for multiclass learning. A negative answer would identify a limit of regularization even when improper prediction is allowed; a positive answer would give a common template for all learnable multiclass classes.
cards.status_note: As of 11 September 2026, two checked preprints claim a negative resolution. Their theorem statements and local-regularization/PAC definitions match the main target, but the full impossibility proofs were not independently audited and no accepted publication was verified. Retained as uncertain rather than certified open or resolved.

cards.definitions: Let X be an instance space, Y a label space that may be infinite, and H⊆Y^X a nonempty class of predictors h:X→Y. A distribution D on labeled examples X×Y is realizable by H if some h*∈H satisfies PrD[h*(x)≠y]=0. The risk of a predictor g is LD(g)=PrD[g(x)≠y]. A learner A maps a finite labeled sample S to a predictor A(S), which need not belong to H. It PAC learns H if, for every ε,δ∈(0,1), there is mA(ε,δ)<∞ such that for every H-realizable D and every m≥mA(ε,δ), a sample S of m independent draws from D satisfies Pr[LD(A(S))>ε]≤δ. Probability spaces, predictors and learners are understood with measurable error events, so these probabilities are defined. There is no running-time requirement. For a nonempty realizable sample S, the version space H[S] consists of all h∈H agreeing with every labeled example in S. A local regularizer assigns each pair (h,x) a nonnegative real score ψ(h,x), fixed before observing S. It is admissible only if a minimum score on H[S] is attained at every test point x and the induced prediction rules are well-defined; an empty argmin cannot make the claim vacuously true. A learner is induced by ψ when A(S)(x) belongs to {h(x): h∈argmin g∈H[S] ψ(g,x)} for every such S,x. On empty or unrealizable samples its behavior is unrestricted. The quantifier “every induced learner” includes every valid tie-breaking rule; its sample bound may depend on that learner. The regularizer can depend on H and x, but not on S, its size, its unlabeled points, D, ε or δ.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every realizably PAC-learnable H has such an admissible regularizer, or give a PAC-learnable class H and prove that every admissible local regularizer induces at least one learner that is not PAC consistent in the stated distribution-independent sense. A favorable tie-breaking rule alone is insufficient. Neither a transductive separation nor failure of proper learning alone settles this PAC question.

context_blocks.title: A different preference at each test point
context_blocks.text: A regularizer expresses which hypotheses the learning rule prefers. Local regularization lets that preference depend on the new point being classified. After training, only hypotheses that fit the sample remain eligible, and the rule predicts using a least-scored eligible hypothesis at that point.

context_blocks.title: Why the prediction can be outside the class
context_blocks.text: One hypothesis might be preferred in one region of X and another in a different region. The resulting predictor can combine their labels without being a single hypothesis from H. This flexibility matters because some multiclass problems are learnable only by allowing such improper output.

context_blocks.title: Ties carry a real quantifier
context_blocks.text: The source asks the regularizer to succeed for every induced tie-breaking learner. If all scores are zero, the rule imposes no preference among sample-consistent hypotheses. Selecting one specially chosen successful learner from those ties would not show that the regularizer itself learns the class. Likewise, score minima must exist for the prediction rule to be meaningful.

context_blocks.title: Sample-dependent regularization is a different model
context_blocks.text: The source reports a general positive result when a local regularizer may first use the unlabeled training points. Here the score function is fixed independently of the sample. The question tests whether that extra sample information is necessary for a general multiclass learning rule.

context_blocks.title: Two 2026 claims of a negative resolution
context_blocks.text: Hou’s July preprint claims a countable learnable class beyond all local regularizers. The August preprint by Asilis and coauthors independently claims a PAC counterexample under the same worst-case tie convention and acknowledges Hou’s work. The checked statements match the main question, but their full lower-bound proofs have not been independently verified in this review. The card therefore records a claimed negative resolution with uncertain status.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
